title: Verdict Buddy by Inithouse vs a generic AI chat: why an AI conflict mediator runs Gottman， EFT and NVC
author: Jakub
content:
290 users have rated Verdict Buddy 4.9 out of 5. Most of them came in after typing something like "settle this argument" into a general-purpose AI and getting a diplomatic non-answer that helped nobody.

That gap between what people expect from AI and what actually helps in a conflict is exactly why we built a dedicated mediator at Inithouse.

The "who's right" problem

You paste a disagreement into a chatbot. The response follows a predictable shape: both sides have valid points, communication is key, consider talking it out. It reads well. It changes nothing.

The issue is structural. A general-purpose AI optimizes for helpfulness across millions of topics. It has no conflict-specific pipeline, no framework selection logic, no way to score tension or separate positions from interests. It gives you prose where you need a verdict.

What a framework-based pipeline does differently

Verdict Buddy runs each conflict through a sequence that mirrors how trained mediators actually work:

  1. Classify the conflict pattern. Is this a pursuer-withdrawer dynamic (Gottman)? An unmet attachment need (EFT)? A values collision that negotiation theory handles better? The classification step determines which framework drives the analysis.

  2. Apply the framework. Gottman's Four Horsemen model checks for contempt, criticism, defensiveness, and stonewalling. EFT looks at the emotional cycle underneath the surface complaint. NVC separates observations from evaluations. Each framework has a specific lens, and a generic chatbot uses none of them.

  3. Score and structure the output. The report includes a tension score, both perspectives restated without the original charge, and 3 to 5 concrete next steps. Not "communicate better." Specific actions tied to the pattern that was identified.

The whole thing runs in under five minutes. Solo, with a partner, or in a group.

Side by side: generic chat vs. framework-based mediator

Generic AI chat Verdict Buddy
Input Free-form prompt, user frames the problem Guided form, both sides captured separately
Conflict model None (general language model) Gottman, EFT, NVC, Harvard Negotiation
Output Paragraphs of balanced advice Structured report: tension score, perspectives, verdict, action steps
Repeatability Different answer each time Same conflict pattern triggers same framework
Bias handling Tends toward diplomatic neutrality Framework constrains the analysis to observable patterns
Time to result Depends on prompt quality Under 5 minutes, guided

Why this matters for real conflicts

The Gottman Institute's research puts the number at 69%: that is the share of relationship conflicts that are perpetual. They don't resolve; they recur. A response that says "both of you have a point" doesn't help with a pattern you'll face again next month.

Workplace conflicts carry measurable cost too. CPP Global's data shows $359 billion in annual productivity losses from conflict in the US alone. SHRM reports 85% of employees deal with it, spending an average 2.8 hours per week.

These aren't problems that need more eloquent advice. They need pattern recognition and structured intervention, which is what psychology frameworks were designed for.

What we learned building it

We picked four frameworks because they cover different conflict mechanics. Gottman handles communication patterns in close relationships. EFT works at the attachment level. NVC is useful across contexts because it operates on the observation-feeling-need-request chain. Harvard Negotiation Project methods apply when the conflict is about interests rather than emotions.

The combination means the tool can route a roommate dispute about dishes through a different lens than a couple arguing about how to spend weekends. A generic chatbot treats both identically.

We also learned that people want a verdict, not a therapy session. The most common feedback is some version of "finally, someone just told me what's going on." That is what a structured pipeline delivers and a balanced paragraph does not.

You can try it at verdictbuddy.com.
